111.quote_or_event: “Impartiality towards all beings in the world, whether friends or enemies, and abstention from injury to living beings throughout the whole life: this is a difficult duty.”
111.explanation: When the prince Mṛgāputra seeks to renounce, his parents warn him that the monk's path demands an even-handed attitude toward friend and foe alike, together with lifelong non-injury.
111.tie_back: Valluvar defines the virtue of fitness as acting rightly toward every group, whether enemies, strangers or friends, and Jain scripture names this same impartiality as one of the hardest duties.
111.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 19.25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; sacred-texts.com)
111._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a near one-to-one match on impartiality toward friend and foe, though the Jain verse frames it as an ascetic's equanimity rather than social justice.

112.explanation: The first of Hemacandra's thirty-five qualities of the ideal Jain householder is wealth acquired by just means (nyāya).
112.tie_back: Valluvar promises that the prosperity of the upright endures, and Jain householder ethics likewise puts justly earned wealth first, though it makes no explicit promise about its lasting for descendants.
112.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra, list of 35 qualities of the ideal śrāvaka, no. 1, as rendered in Vilas A. Sangave, 'Prescription of Ethical Code' (jainworld.com)
112._accuracy_note: Verified on Sangave's jainworld page (a secondary rendering). It matches the just acquisition of wealth, but not the Kural's claim that such wealth endures as a support for descendants.

113.quote_or_event: “The consequences of violence, falsehood, stealing, unchastity and attachment are calamity and reproach in this world and in the next birth.”
113.explanation: Umāsvāti teaches that whatever is gained by breaching the vows, including taking what is not rightly one's own, brings disaster and disgrace both now and hereafter.
113.tie_back: Valluvar says gain won by abandoning fairness must be given up that very day even if it seems to bring only good, and the Tattvārtha Sūtra explains why: such gain carries calamity in this life and the next.
113._accuracy_note: Verified on jainworld's Tattvārtha Sūtra page (not Tatia's translation). It fits thematically, but it concerns the vows in general rather than impartiality, and lacks the Kural's 'renounce it that very day'.

114.quote_or_event: “My own Self is the doer and undoer of misery and happiness; my own Self, friend and foe, according as I act well or badly.”
114.explanation: The monk Anāthin tells King Śreṇika that each person's condition is the result of their own good or bad conduct, with no outside protector.
114.tie_back: Valluvar says a person's justice or injustice shows in what they leave behind, and Jain karma doctrine likewise holds that what follows a person is simply the fruit of acting well or badly.
114.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 20.37 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; sacred-texts.com)
114._accuracy_note: Next-best match only. The quote is verified, but Jain doctrine locates a person's results in their own karma, not in descendants or posthumous reputation, so the Kural's 'what remains' (echcham) has no direct Jain counterpart.

115.quote_or_event: “He was indifferent to success or failure (in begging), to happiness and misery, to life and death, to blame and praise, to honour and insult.”
115.explanation: Mṛgāputra, once a monk, holds the same even mind whether things go well or badly.
115.tie_back: Valluvar grants that loss and gain will come and calls the unbent heart the ornament of the noble, and this verse shows the Jain ideal of a mind that stays level through both.
115.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 19.90 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; sacred-texts.com)
115._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a strong fit on equanimity amid gain and loss, though the Jain verse stresses detachment rather than the Kural's fairness in judgment.

116.quote_or_event: “A cut-throat enemy will not do him such harm as his own perversity will do him; the man without pity will feel repentance in the hour of death.”
116.explanation: The sermon to King Śreṇika warns that a person's own inner corruption ruins them more surely than any outside foe.
116.tie_back: Valluvar asks one whose heart turns from fairness to recognise it as the sign of their own ruin, and the Uttarādhyayana likewise names the perverted heart as the real destroyer.
116.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 20.48 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; sacred-texts.com)
116._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a good fit on self-inflicted ruin, though the context is a lapsed monk rather than partiality. Jacobi notes that verses 38-53 may be a later addition.

117.quote_or_event: “The good, though they be poor and emaciated, will not guiltily ascend and rise over the bounds (of duty); binding their courage, as much as in them lies, with the cords of a mind free from anxiety, they will do the things that ought to be done.”
117.explanation: The Nālaḍiyār describes the good as keeping within the bounds of right conduct even in poverty, unashamed and steady.
117.tie_back: Valluvar says the world does not count the poverty of one who holds to fairness as a downfall, and the Nālaḍiyār shows such a person poor in means yet unbroken in duty.
117.source: Nālaḍiyār ch. 16 'The Good', st. 3 (= st. 153), English translation in The Indian Antiquary (wisdomlib.org)
117._accuracy_note: A Tamil Jain text, chosen because it addresses the just person's poverty directly; it describes the good person's steadiness rather than the world's verdict on them.

118.quote_or_event: “He, in whom attachment and aversion do not create any disturbance, (is said to have) steadfast equanimity, according to the preaching of the omniscient.”
118.explanation: Kundakunda defines true equanimity (sāmāyika) as a mind that neither attachment nor aversion can tip.
118.tie_back: Valluvar's balance-beam first sets itself level and leans to neither side, and Kundakunda's sage, unmoved by attachment or aversion, is that balance in Jain terms.
118.source: Kundakunda, Niyamasāra 9.128 'Supreme Equanimity' (English rendering on jainworld.com)
118._accuracy_note: Verified on jainworld. Rāga and dveṣa (attachment and aversion) are precisely the two 'sides' toward which a judge leans, but the text concerns inner spiritual equanimity, not the act of judging others.

119.quote_or_event: “Crooked and deceptive actions of mind, speach and body, and criticising the right actions and prompting for wrong actions cause the influx of inauspicious physique-making karmas.” The next sutra adds: “The opposites of these (namely straightforward activity and honestry or candour) cause the influx of auspicious physique-making karmas.”
119.explanation: Umāsvāti names crookedness (yoga-vakratā) as a single fault running through mind, speech and body together, and its cure as straightforwardness (ārjava) in all three.
119.tie_back: Valluvar says straight speech is true rectitude only if the heart is also unbent, and the Tattvārtha Sūtra likewise treats crookedness of mind and of speech as one fault to be removed together.
119._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on jainworld, including the source's misspellings ('speach', 'honestry'). It is a good fit on the inner/outer crookedness pairing, though framed as karmic causation rather than a test of fairness.

120.quote_or_event: “Prompting others to steal, receiving stolen goods, underbuying in a disordered state, using false weights and measures, and deceiving others with artificial or imitation goods are the five transgressions of non-stealing.”
120.explanation: The Jain layperson's vow of non-stealing explicitly forbids false weights and measures and adulterated goods, which binds merchants to honest dealing.
120.tie_back: Valluvar says the true way of trade is to guard others' interests as one's own, and the Jain householder vow writes this into commerce by forbidding cheating in weights, measures and goods.
120._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on jainworld (not Tatia's translation); a close and specific fit for honest trade, phrased as a prohibition rather than the Kural's positive 'as their own'.
